title: Detect and Remove Loop in Linked List
statement:
You are given the head of a singly linked list that may contain a loop: the `next` pointer of the last node may point back to an earlier node of the list instead of being null.

Detect whether the list contains a loop and, if it does, **remove it** by setting the `next` pointer of the last node of the loop to null, so that the list becomes a plain list that ends normally. Every node must stay in the list.

In the test input the loop is described by `pos`: the index (0-based, counted from the head) of the node that the last node of the list points to, or `-1` if the list has no loop. Your function does not receive `pos`; it only receives the head node, so the loop has to be found from the structure of the list (for example with Floyd's tortoise and hare). Node values may repeat, so nodes are identified by position, not by value.

Report two things: the index of the node where the loop begins (the first node of the loop that is reached from the head), or `-1` if there is no loop; and the values of the list after the loop has been removed, read from the head until the list ends.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`, the number of nodes.
The second line contains `n` integers: the node values from head to tail.
The third line contains the integer `pos` (`-1` for no loop, otherwise `0 ≤ pos ≤ n - 1`): the last node's `next` points to the node at index `pos`.
outputFormat:
The first line: the index of the node where the loop begins, or `-1` if there is no loop.
The second line: the `n` values of the list after loop removal, from head to tail, separated by spaces.

examples.explanation: The last node (value 5) points back to the node at index 2 (value 4), so the loop is 4 -> 1 -> 5 -> 4. The loop starts at index 2. Cutting the pointer out of the last node leaves the list 3 -> 1 -> 4 -> 1 -> 5.
The last node points to null, so there is no loop and the list is unchanged.
The last node points to itself, a loop of length one that starts at index 2. Removing it sets that node's `next` to null.

hints: A slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two steps will meet inside the loop if one exists, and the fast pointer reaches null otherwise.
After they meet, put one pointer back at the head and move both one step at a time: they meet again exactly at the first node of the loop.
To cut the loop you need the node whose `next` is the loop start. Keep walking one pointer around the loop from the start until its `next` is the start.
